According to CIA records, a Soviet citizen observed a bright green circular object or mass in the sky west of Site 7 at Sary Shagan in late summer 1973 [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA]. The object was positioned at an angle of sighting of approximately 70 degrees, though its altitude could not be determined. The observer believed the green mass would have been higher than cloud level, despite there being no clouds that evening.

Within 10 to 15 seconds of observation, the green circle widened and several green concentric circles formed around the mass. Within minutes, the coloring disappeared. There was no sound, such as an explosion, associated with the phenomenon [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA]. The observer could not estimate the diameter of the object [UNDATED-CIA-158652].

The sighting occurred while the observer had stepped outside for some air during a televised sport competition between Canada and the USSR [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA].

The archive contains two distinct records about the Tremonton film from July 2, 1952.

The primary record [1952-USN-80203D] documents that Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filmed approximately 30 feet of 16mm color motion picture film showing a group of 10-12 unidentified objects milling about in rough formation proceeding westerly. The filming occurred at 1110 MST seven miles north of Tremonton, Utah, on U.S. Highway 30S. Newhouse was driving from Washington, D.C., to Portland, Oregon, when his wife noticed the objects. He used a Bell and Howell Auto Master camera with a three inch telephoto lens, hand-held, shooting at sixteen frames per second. The first few feet were taken at one f-stop, with the balance at a different setting. One object reversed course and was tracked separately across the camera field of view multiple times. This case remains unresolved.

A second record [1952-DOW-141453] covers the same incident but with different details. It states that two photographs were taken, though the objects appeared too small on film to show detail. This record characterizes the resolution as "identified," contrasting with the unresolved status in the Navy record.

The archive evidence shows these records belong to different canonical events (evt-0585 and evt-0586) and come from different source documents, suggesting they represent separate institutional assessments of the same incident.

The December 12, 1948 green fireball was reported near Starvation Peak (Bernal, New Mexico) and Los Alamos, New Mexico [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]. The object was observed simultaneously from two stations in New Mexico. According to the official record, it appeared at approximately latitude 35° 50', longitude 106° 40' and disappeared near latitude 35° 45', longitude 107°, traversing a nearly horizontal path of approximately 25 miles at an altitude of 8 to 10 miles above the surface.

On 19 November 1968, the USS Clyatt detected an unidentified object on radar in the vicinity of Puerto Rico [1968-USN-6F2707]. According to the record, the object appeared on the Clyatt's radar for twenty-one seconds and closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles distance. The record does not provide further details about the object's characteristics or the outcome of the detection, and the incident remains classified as unresolved.

According to the archive evidence, a potato-shaped, creamy-white translucent object with articulating panels was observed over the Cheyenne Mountains in the Colorado Springs 2022 narrative [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]. 

A former U.S. Army intelligence officer and four members of his unit witnessed the object as they exited their office building. The object had distinct edges and appeared painted in a creamy/whitish opalescent color. After remaining still for approximately two minutes, the object vanished with what the witness described as a cloaking effect [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

According to the FBI material, the November 2021 sighting involved lights that formed a **triangular pattern**. The witness initially observed a singular light that split into two or three lights, which then arranged themselves in a triangular pattern with a light in the center [UNDATED-FBI-380101]. The observation lasted approximately ten minutes before the lights disappeared after an accidental camera flash.

The archive documents a significant wave of sightings over Scandinavia in 1946, known as the "ghost rockets" phenomenon.

According to the archive, flying missiles were first reported over southern Sweden in late May 1946, with the press giving them the name "Ghost Rockets" [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896]. By June, the missiles had also been reported over Finland and Denmark, and by July the number of sightings over Sweden had greatly increased, with several also reported over Norway [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896]. Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports during this period, which extended from late May through October 1946 [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

Witnesses described the objects in varied terms. Some reports characterized them as "a ball of fire with a tail" or "shiny cigar-shaped objects" [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896]. A separate NASA source describes the objects from February to December 1946 as "generally fusiform objects (occasionally resembling spheres or disks) flying most often horizontally in Swedish skies, in some cases leaving a luminous trail, but also capable of very suddenly ascending or descending" [1946-NASA-A146CF].

The phenomenon caused concern among military authorities in multiple nations [1946-NASA-A146CF]. The archive records one fragment as having an "identified" resolution [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896], while another lists the same general phenomenon as "unresolved" [1946-NASA-A146CF], though the evidence does not explain this discrepancy or provide details about what identification, if any, was reached.

On the night of 19 November, a Crusader pilot observed a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter in full moonlight with good visibility near Puerto Rico [1968-USN-85858D]. The object's estimated speed exceeded Mach 3.

This observation occurred the same day that the USS Clyatt detected an unidentified object on radar that appeared for twenty-one seconds and closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles distance [1968-USN-6F2707].

In the triangular object case near Baku, a U.S. tourist and three companions aboard a train observed a large triangular object on an airfield approximately two miles away, between the train and the Caspian Sea coast, about 50-65 miles south of Baku, Azerbaijan on October 4, 1955 [1955-CIA-E34C6D].

The object was described as comparable in size to a U.S. jet fighter, with a squat shape in the form of an equilateral triangle. It had three lights, one on each point of the triangle, which the observer presumed were two wing lights and a tail light. A huge searchlight on the field illuminated the triangular object on the ground [1955-CIA-E34C6D].

According to the report, the object "was ejected from its launching site, making not less than three and not more than seven fast spirals in the air, after which it climbed extremely fast at about a 45 degree angle." The searchlight tracked the object as it climbed [1955-CIA-E34C6D].

The case remains unresolved in the archive records.

According to CIA material, an unidentified object was observed hovering at high altitude over Harare International Airport on the afternoon of July 2, 2008 [2008-CIA-052DE8]. The object was detected by what appears to have been both radar and optical means. It was described as disc-like with rotating lights on its underside, and it shifted colors before quickly ascending out of visual range [2008-CIA-052DE8]. The observation remained unresolved.

The January 30, 1949 Socorro green fireball record describes a green fireball that occurred in the Socorro, New Mexico area [1949-USAF-5C0132]. Despite air and ground searches conducted in early February along what the record calls "the well determined earth-trace" of the fireball, no fragments were recovered [1949-USAF-5C0132]. The searches were systematic efforts to locate physical material from the event, but they were unsuccessful.

The Tremonton film fragments should be described as **one filming episode**, not several unrelated events.

Newhouse filmed approximately 30 feet of 16mm color motion picture film on July 2, 1952, at 1110 MST, seven miles north of Tremonton, Utah, on U.S. Highway 30S. During this single filming episode, he captured a group of 10-12 unidentified objects milling about in rough formation proceeding westerly. Within this same filming sequence, one object reversed course and was tracked separately across the camera field of view multiple times.

The evidence indicates this was a continuous filming event that began when Newhouse's wife noticed the objects and he retrieved his Bell and Howell camera. The first few feet were filmed at one f-stop setting (F8) and the balance at another (F16), all at sixteen frames per second, documenting the objects' behavior during a single observation period. The fact that one object broke from the formation and was tracked separately does not constitute a separate event—it describes the behavior of objects during the same filming episode.

The Puerto Rico November 1968 records share several common elements. All three incidents occurred within a five-day period in the vicinity of Puerto Rico and involved U.S. Navy operations with fighter aircraft.

On 19 November, two separate observations took place. The USS Clyatt detected an unidentified object on radar that appeared for twenty-one seconds and closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles [1968-USN-6F2707]. That same night, a Crusader pilot visually observed a delta-shaped object approximately the size of a jet fighter in full moonlight with good visibility, with the object's estimated speed exceeding Mach 3 [1968-USN-85858D].

Five days later on 24 November, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target that rapidly pulled away from a Crusader aircraft flying at Mach 0.99 at 45,000 feet [1968-USN-9E57C2].

All three cases remained unresolved according to the records. They share common characteristics of high performance capabilities, involvement with Navy fighter operations (particularly Crusader aircraft), and detection through either radar or visual observation under favorable conditions.

Dr. Lincoln LaPaz at the University of New Mexico investigated these objects, which were reported as brilliant greenish-blue in color with definite flat trajectories, unlike typical meteors [UNDATED-USAF-B32231]. The reports noted that these fireballs "don't explode" despite their apparent low altitude and size.

Two specific 1949 events are documented. On January 30, 1949, a green fireball occurred over the Socorro, New Mexico area [1949-USAF-5C0132]. Despite air and ground searches in early February along what was described as "the well determined earth-trace" of this fireball, no fragments were recovered. A second event occurred on July 24, 1949, when a bright green fireball passed over Socorro at 8:26 p.m. [1949-USAF-9D1046]. Systematic collections of airborne material were attempted to recover particles from this event.

Additional observations noted distinctive features. One green fireball on December 12 came in at high angles to the horizontal, different from Geminid meteors observed the same night [UNDATED-DOE-80EBE8]. A Texas green fireball on January 30 was described as having brightness comparable to the moon and exhibited horizontal flight [UNDATED-DOE-5FC004].

Color observations varied by viewing angle. One object seen on a Sunday night appeared bronze-colored from Kirtland Field tower but was reported as green from Arizona until it turned straight down [UNDATED-USAF-6A96A7].

The reports do not provide definitive explanations for these phenomena, with most remaining unresolved.
